summary: Yes, both spectra show graphene, and I read it as monolayer or turbostratic graphene because each has a single-Lorentzian 2D band at about 37–40 cm⁻¹ FWHM. The 2D band is more intense than G by about 2.0 (Cu) to 2.8 (Au). The two layers differ in two ways: (1) graphene on Au is clearly more defective, with I_D/I_G of about 1 against about 0.55 on Cu, and (2) the 2D band sits about 16 cm⁻¹ higher on Cu (about 2697 cm⁻¹) than on Au (2681 cm⁻¹) while G does not move. Shifted 2D with unshifted G points to compressive strain, or to coupling with the Cu surface, rather than simple doping. The laser wavelength is not in the file, so I assumed about 532 nm. The D position (1344 cm⁻¹ on Au) and the 2D position are consistent with that assumption, but they do not prove it.

observations.finding: Both spectra contain the graphene D, G and 2D bands, so a graphene-type sp² layer is present on both metals. Neither spectrum shows Au or Cu Raman bands, which is expected because the metals have no first-order Raman signal.
observations.evidence: Au: D 1344.3±1.1 (FWHM 35±4), G 1580.4±0.8 (FWHM 26±3), 2D 2681.3±0.4 (FWHM 39.7±1.2). Cu: D 1348±5 (FWHM ~27), G 1581±3 (FWHM ~27), 2D 2696–2698±1.4 (FWHM 32–37±4). Fits are Lorentzian plus a local polynomial background; fit residuals match the noise (rms ~17 counts on Au, ~9 on Cu).

observations.finding: The layer is most likely a single layer, or electronically decoupled (turbostratic) layers, on both metals. The 2D band is one symmetric Lorentzian with no multi-component structure, and it is stronger than G.
observations.evidence: I_2D/I_G (peak height above baseline) is 2.8 on Au (323–340 / 116) and 2.0–2.1 on Cu (48–49 / 23–24). Area ratio A_2D/A_G is 4.5 on Au and 2.9–3.2 on Cu. A single Lorentzian describes 2D on both within noise, and a second component at 2684 on Au or 2677 on Cu has no weight (FWHM pinned at the 4 cm⁻¹ bound). On Cu the ratio is uncertain because G is small and noisy.
observations.source: Ferrari et al., PRL 97, 187401 (2006), Fig. 1 and discussion of the single-Lorentzian 2D band. Ferrari & Basko, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235 (2013), Fig. 2.

observations.finding: Graphene on Au is considerably more defective than on Cu. The D band is about as strong as G on Au and only about half of G on Cu.
observations.evidence: I_D/I_G is 111/116 = 0.96 on Au, with area ratio 1.3, and 13/24 = 0.55 on Cu, with area ratio ~0.6. The Cu value is uncertain because the D band is only about 1.5× the per-point noise. A 1.7-fold or greater difference in I_D/I_G is far outside the fit errors. D' (~1620) is not resolved on either metal. D+G (~2940) is not significant on either. A weak 2D' (~3248) appears only on Au, and only marginally.

observations.finding: Both layers are in the low-defect-density regime (stage 1), where I_D/I_G increases with defect density. This is supported by the strong 2D band, the narrow G band (26 cm⁻¹) and the absence of a resolved D'. Taking the measured I_D/I_G as is, the mean inter-defect distance is about 12 nm on Au and about 16 nm on Cu, assuming 532 nm. These values are only indicative.
observations.evidence: L_D² = 1.8×10⁻⁹ · λ⁴ / (I_D/I_G). With λ = 532 nm and I_D/I_G = 0.96 this gives L_D ≈ 12 nm. With I_D/I_G = 0.55 it gives L_D ≈ 16 nm. The formula was calibrated on ion-bombarded graphene on SiO₂ at 514 nm and rescaled by λ⁴. Metal substrate enhancement and the unknown wavelength are not corrected for.
observations.source: Cançado et al., Nano Lett. 11, 3190 (2011), Eq. 4 and Fig. 3. Lucchese et al., Carbon 48, 1592 (2010), Fig. 1 for the stage-1 and stage-2 behaviour.

observations.finding: The 2D band is about 16 cm⁻¹ higher on Cu than on Au, while G is the same within error. G is also slightly below the usual ~1582 cm⁻¹ on both metals. On Au, 2D and G are close to values for relaxed, lightly doped graphene at ~532 nm. Graphene on Cu therefore carries something that shifts 2D but not G. The likely cause is biaxial compressive strain from differential thermal contraction of the substrate on quenching, plus interaction with the Cu surface. The data do not separate the two.
observations.evidence: Δω_2D = 2697 − 2681 ≈ +16 cm⁻¹ (error ~1.5). Δω_G = 1581±2.6 − 1580.4±0.8 ≈ +0.6±3 cm⁻¹. For biaxial strain the 2D shift is roughly 2.2× the G shift (Mohiuddin et al. report ∂ω_2D/∂ε about 2.2 times ∂ω_G/∂ε in magnitude). A 16 cm⁻¹ shift from strain alone would then give a G shift of roughly +6 to +7 cm⁻¹, which the data disfavour at about 2σ. A cancelling doping contribution, or Cu coupling that affects 2D differently from G, would reconcile this. Pure hole doping is unlikely because I_2D/I_G stays above 2.
observations.source: Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024 (2012), Fig. 3 (strain and doping vector analysis). Mohiuddin et al., PRB 79, 205433 (2009), Table I (Grüneisen parameters). Das et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 3, 210 (2008), Figs. 2–3 (doping dependence of G, 2D and their ratio).

observations.finding: The absolute signal and background differ strongly between the two metals, so the absolute intensities cannot be compared. Au shows a 2D peak height of about 330 counts on a 1000–1500 count rising background. Cu shows about 49 counts on a 620–800 count background.
observations.evidence: The Au background rises from ~1000 to ~1500 counts across the range. The Cu background rises from ~620 to ~820 and falls again. The 2D peak height is about 7× larger on Au. The causes cannot be separated from these data: possible plasmonic enhancement on Au, differences in focus or coupling, layer coverage, or laser alignment on a small droplet.

properties.value: 1 (or turbostratic multilayer behaving as monolayer) on both Au and Cu

properties.source: Cançado et al., Nano Lett. 11, 3190 (2011), Eq. 4

properties.value: Low doping on both (I_2D/I_G > 2, G near 1580); sign not determined

properties.value: sp² graphene with no evidence of amorphous carbon (G FWHM ~26 cm⁻¹, no broad D+G background)

caveats: The laser wavelength is unknown. D and 2D are dispersive (D shifts ~50 cm⁻¹/eV and 2D ~100 cm⁻¹/eV), and I_D/I_G scales as λ⁻⁴. Absolute positions, the L_D numbers and the strain reasoning all depend on the 532 nm assumption. The comparison of the two spectra holds if they were taken at the same wavelength, which I assumed.

The Cu spectrum is noisy (D peak ~13 counts above baseline, ~1.5× the per-point noise), so the Cu D/G ratio, D width and any D' are poorly determined. The conclusion that Au is more defective is robust. The exact Cu defect density is not.

Measuring on the metal means no SiO₂ reference, with possible chemical or electronic coupling to the metal and possible electromagnetic enhancement. I_D/I_G and I_2D/I_G from graphene on metals are not directly comparable with the SiO₂-calibrated literature relations.

The strain interpretation is not unique. A 16 cm⁻¹ 2D shift with no G shift is not what pure biaxial strain predicts. Doping, Cu-graphene coupling, local Cu-induced rippling, or a different local graphene orientation relative to the Cu lattice could contribute. The G error on Cu (±2.6 cm⁻¹) is large enough that mild strain is not excluded.

Strain does not necessarily arise from quenching alone. Graphene grown on liquid or solid metal can also be strained by wrinkles, by contraction of the metal during solidification and by lattice coupling. Au and Cu differ in thermal expansion, solidification behaviour, grain structure and carbon solubility, but these data cannot say which of them matters.

The higher defect level on Au is consistent with, but not proven to come from, the high ethylene flux and fast growth, which would give many nuclei and many grain boundaries. Edges, grain boundaries, sp³ sites and vacancies all give D intensity and cannot be told apart from one spectrum. The unresolved D' only weakly disfavours vacancy-dominated damage.

Single spot per sample. It is unknown whether the spectra are representative of the whole droplet. Droplet curvature, partial coverage and focus on a curved surface can change both intensity and apparent ratios.
Au interband emission and Cu background luminescence were handled with a local polynomial baseline. The baseline model affects peak heights by several percent and has little effect on positions.
questions_for_user: What was the laser wavelength? It fixes the absolute positions of D and 2D, which allow a proper strain and doping assignment, and it fixes the L_D conversion.
Were the Au and Cu spectra acquired with the same laser and objective? A different wavelength would explain part of a 2D shift of this size, so the comparison depends on it.
Is the Cu droplet solid or liquid at measurement? Is the Au droplet solid? The solidified metal's grain orientation and thermal contraction decide the strain transferred to the graphene.
Was the graphene coverage continuous or in islands on each droplet? What are the typical grain sizes from SEM or LEED? That separates a high defect density from a high grain-boundary density.
Do you have maps or several points per droplet? That would show whether the 2D position (strain) and I_D/I_G vary spatially, for example near the droplet edge.
Do you have a transferred-to-SiO₂ reference of the same graphene? It would separate substrate effects (strain from the metal, coupling) from intrinsic quality.

limits: Cannot determine layer number beyond 'monolayer-like' (single-Lorentzian 2D), because turbostratic multilayers look similar.
Cannot separate strain from doping or from Cu-graphene coupling with only one wavelength and the G and 2D positions.
Cannot identify the type of defect (vacancies, sp³, edges, grain boundaries) or the grain size from this Raman data alone.
Cannot say how representative one spot is, or compare absolute intensities between Au and Cu.
Cannot confirm the laser wavelength; the 532 nm assumption is consistent with the data but not proven.
Cannot determine the crystallographic orientation of the graphene relative to the metal, or whether it was grown on liquid or on solid metal.
